10-024.r: Vikrama Samvat → began 57 BC (also called Krit and Malav Samvat); Jain texts put it 470 years after Mahavira's salvation (527 BC).

10-025.r: Saka year = AD year minus 78 → December 2009 = Saka 1931; Saka Samvat is India's national calendar.

10-026.r: Kanishka's contemporaries → Ashvaghosa (court poet; Buddhacharita, Saundaranand) and Vasumitra (headed the Fourth Buddhist Council). Kalidas was Gupta-era; Kamban not contemporary.

10-028.r: Kanishka's court → Parsva, Vasumitra, Ashvaghosa, Nagarjuna, Charaka (court physician), Mathara. Patanjali (Mahabhasya) was Shunga-era; Vishakhadatta also not in his court.
10-028.t: Don't confuse Charaka (Kanishka's physician) with Patanjali (Shunga period).

10-030.r: Rabatak inscription of Kanishka (found 1993 in Afghanistan; Greek script, Bactrian language) → names Saket, Kaushambi, Pataliputra, Sri Champa; not Shravasti.
10-030.h: Four cities 'SKPC': Saket, Kaushambi, Pataliputra, Champa.

10-031.r: Taxila-educated Ayurvedacharyas → Charaka and Jivaka (Bimbisara's physician); Kautilya, Chandragupta Maurya, Prasenjit and Vasubandhu also studied there. Both (c) and (d) correct.

10-032.r: Dynasties in order → Maurya (321-185 BCE), Shunga (185-73 BCE), Kanva (73-28 BCE), Kushan (1st-3rd century CE).
10-032.h: M-S-K-K: Maurya, Shunga, Kanva, then Kushan.

10-033.r: Ayodhya inscription → records two Ashwamedha yajnas by Pushyamitra Shunga, who founded the Shunga dynasty by killing Brihadratha (185 BCE).

10-034.r: Shungas' ancestors → from Ujjain; last Shunga ruler Devabhuti was killed by his minister (Amatya) Vasudeva Kanva.

10-035.r: After the Shungas → Kanva dynasty (Vasudeva Kanva killed Devabhuti); Kanvas were Brahmins like the Shungas.

10-036.r: Gautamiputra Satakarni → 'protector of the Varna system' (Nashik inscription): stopped inter-mixing of the four varnas; patron of Brahmanism.

10-037.r: Most powerful dynasty of the South after the Mauryas → Satavahanas, founded by Simuka (Sindhuk) after killing Kanva king Susharman.

10-039.r: Chinese general Pan Chao → defeated Kanishka's force after the Han princess marriage request was refused (Chinese texts, 73-94 AD).

10-040.r: Empires extending outside India → Kushana (Kanishka: Turpan in China, Afghanistan to Bihar) and Maurya (parts of modern Iran). Both (b) and (c) correct.

10-041.r: Child marriage → began in the Kushana period (1st century); Upanayana for girls ended; age 8-10 thought best for a girl's marriage.

10-042.r: Sixteen coins of Indo-Greek King Menander → found at Bairat.

10-043.r: Kushans → Gandhara School of Art (Indo-Greek style, Greek-influenced, patronised by Kanishka).
10-043.t: Ajanta paintings are not Mughal and Pahari painting is not Maratha; only Kushan-Gandhara is right.

10-045.r: Gold-silver coin ratio in the Shaka-Kshatrapa period → 1:35.

10-046.r: Satavahanas → no gold coins (lead, copper, bronze, silver, potin). Kushanas → gold, copper; Guptas → gold, silver; Kalachuris → gold, silver, copper.
10-046.t: Satavahanas are known for lead and potin coins, not gold.

10-047.r: Gandhara Art → Kushanas; Junagarh Rock inscription → Rudradaman I; Milindapanho → Menander; Taxila inscription → Patika.

10-048.r: Bamiyan (Afghanistan) → Buddha statues cut into the hills, destroyed by the Taliban.

10-049.r: Gandhara art → blend of Indian and Greek (also Syrian, Persian) styles; Saka-Kushan era; called Greco-Buddhist or Indo-Greek art; subject only the Buddha.

10-052.r: Gandhara sculptures → invariably used green schist as medium; strongly influenced by Greek sculpture.

10-054.r: Darius I (522-486 BC) → first Persian ruler to capture part of India (lands around the Indus, per Herodotus).

10-055.r: Earliest dynasty among Chalukya, Pallava, Rashtrakuta, Satavahana → Satavahana, founded by Simuk around the second century BC.

10-056.r: Matsya Purana → longest list of Andhra-Satavahana kings (30 rulers).

10-057.r: Satavahana capital → Paithan (Pratishthan) as main capital; initial capital believed to be Amravati; founder Simuka.
10-057.t: Both Amravati (early) and Pratishthan (main) appear as book answers; pick whichever is offered.

10-059.r: 'Ekabrahmana' (unrivalled Brahmana) → Gautamiputra Shatakarni, in his mother Gautami Balashri's Nashik inscription.

10-060.r: Shunga → Pataliputra; Satavahana → Paithan (Pratishthan); Kadamba → Banvasi; Chandel → Mahoba.

10-061.r: Karnasuvarna → West Bengal (Murshidabad); Pragjyotisha → Assam; Girnar → Gujarat; Pratishthana (Paithan, on Godavari) → Maharashtra.

10-062.r: Order → Satavahanas (Simuk, first century BC), Vakatakas (Vindhyashakti, third century AD), Chalukyas of Gujarat (Mulraj I, tenth century AD).

10-063.r: Satavahana period → Sanskrit, Prakrit and folk languages developed, as the kings promoted them for literary writing; A and R true, R explains A.

10-064.r: Satavahana kings → nurtured Prakrit (more than Sanskrit); public aspect of art encouraged, mostly Buddhist. Both statements correct.

10-065.r: Vakatakas rose after the Satavahanas weakened; founder → Vindhyashakti; Pravarasena I was his son. Only statement (i) true.
10-065.t: Founder is Vindhyashakti, not Pravarasena I (his son).

10-066.r: Amaravati Stupa (Andhra Pradesh) → platform with Ayaka (Aryak) pillars.

10-067.r: Wrong pair: Bhitari pillar (Ghazipur, UP) → Skandagupta, not Pulakeshin II (Aihole inscription). Correct: Nasik → Gautamiputra; Hathigumpha → Kharavela; Girnar → Rudradaman I.

10-068.r: Ikshvakus → called 'Shriparvatiya' in the Puranas; feudatories of the Satavahanas who became independent; founder Shrisantmula.

10-069.r: Kushanas traded via the Persian Gulf and Red Sea (Periplus, Arikamedu evidence) → A true; no evidence of a Kushana navy → R false.

10-070.r: Kharavela (Chedi dynasty, king of Kalinga, Odisha) → Hathigumpha inscription in Udayagiri caves; patron of Jainism.

10-074.r: Kharavela of Kalinga → Mahameghavahana dynasty, also called Chedi dynasty by some scholars; more than one option fits, so (e).

10-075.r: Hathigumpha inscription (Udayagiri, near Bhubaneswar, Odisha) → main source on Kalinga ruler Kharavela.

10-076.r: Udayagiri (18 caves) and Khandagiri (15 caves), Bhubaneswar → both natural and artificial caves; Hathigumpha inscription is in Udayagiri, not Khandagiri.

10-077.r: Justinian (Eastern Roman ruler) → famous for Roman law; his Corpus Juris Civilis is still a base of civil law.

10-078.r: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea → anonymous work (mid first century CE) by a Greek-speaking merchant; not Pliny, Ptolemy, Strabo or Ctesias, so (e).

10-079.r: Ancient India had many river ports and large entrepots of goods and traffic (Lothal, Muziris, Sopara); both statements correct.

11-001.r: Gupta rule → c. 275-550 AD (founder Srigupta); first powerful ruler Chandragupta I (319-335 AD, title 'Maharajadhiraja'); best option 319-500 AD.

11-002.r: Vakataka king Pravarasena I → performed four Ashwamedhas; Pravarasena II wrote 'Setubandha'.
11-002.t: Don't confuse Pravarasena I (four Ashwamedhas) with Pravarasena II (author of Setubandha).

11-003.r: V.A. Smith ('Early History of India') → called Samudragupta (335-375 AD) the 'Napoleon of India' for his military conquests.

11-005.r: Chandragupta II 'Vikramaditya' → also called Devagupta, Devaraja (Sanchi inscription) and Devashri.

11-006.r: Samudragupta → first Gupta ruler to take the title 'Param Bhagavata' (Nalanda and Gaya copper plates).
11-006.t: UPPSC's key gave Chandragupta II; the book and UGC accept Samudragupta.

11-008.r: Allahabad Pillar → Ashokan pillar (first at Kaushambi, moved by Akbar) carrying Samudragupta's Prayag Prashasti by Harisena in Sanskrit, listing his conquests.

11-011.r: Prayag Prashasti of Samudragupta → Mahendra was the king of Kosala (a Dakshinapath kingdom).

11-012.r: Allahabad (Prayag) pillar → four inscriptions: Ashoka's (Brahmi), Queen Karuvaki's edict, Samudragupta's by Harisena (Sanskrit, Brahmi), and Jahangir's (Persian).

11-013.r: Samudragupta → 'Lichchhavi-Dauhitra' (daughter's son of the Lichchhavis); mother Kumaradevi was a Lichchhavi princess; father Chandragupta I.

11-014.r: Samudragupta → after his Ashvamedha took the title 'Prithivyah Pratiratha' (no rival on earth / first hero of the Earth).
11-014.c: UPPSC excluded this question from evaluation; the book's title wording ('Prithivyama Pratiratha') differs from the question's.

11-015.r: Harisena → court poet and minister of Samudragupta, wrote the Prayag Prashasti; 'Devichandraguptam' is by Vishakhadatta. Statements 1 and 3 correct.

11-016.r: Samudragupta's southern rivals: Dhananjaya → Kusthalpura; Nilaraja → Avamukta; Ugrasena → Palaka; Vishnugopa → Kanchi.

11-017.r: Mehrauli Iron Pillar (Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, Delhi) → inscription of king 'Chandra' = Chandragupta II; first set up at Vishnugiri near Udaigiri around 410 AD.
